title: Efficient LLM Serving Under Variable Cloud Traffic Loads

first_sections.title: Rise of LLMs in Cloud-Based Production Systems
Challenges of Variable Traffic in LLM Serving
Traffic Monitoring and Feature Extraction Layer

paragraph_samples.text_preview: The past few years have witnessed an unprecedented surge in the deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) across a wide spectrum of real-world applications. From intelligent virtual assistants and automated customer support systems to AI-powered code generation tools and clinical decision support platforms, LLMs have fundamentally transformed how software systems interact with human users. Models such as GPT-4, LLaMA-3, Gemini, and Claude have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in natural language understanding, multi-step reasoning, and open-ended text generation, driving massive adoption

Cloud platforms have emerged as the primary infrastructure backbone for hosting and serving these models at scale. The elastic nature of cloud computing, combined with access to high-performance GPU clusters, makes it an ideal environment for deploying LLM-powered services to millions of concurrent users globally. Major cloud providers such as Amazon Web Services (AWS), Google Cloud Platform (GCP), and Microsoft Azure have each invested heavily in building dedicated AI inference infrastructure.

According to recent industry reports, the global market for cloud-based AI inference is projected to exceed $150 billion by 2028, with LLM serving constituting the fastest-growing segment. Enterprises across all sectors are increasingly building their core product experiences on top of LLM APIs, creating a new class of latencysensitive, throughput-demanding AI services that must operate reliably at scale, around the clock, and under constantly shifting user demand patterns.

Traffic variability is a fundamental characteristic of any large-scale internet service, and LLM serving systems are no exception. Real-world LLM deployments experience multiple forms of traffic variability, each presenting distinct and compounding challenges to the serving infrastructure.

User activity naturally follows time-of-day cycles, with peak usage concentrated during business hours and significantly lower traffic overnight and on weekends. Static GPU allocations sized for peak load result in massive resource waste during off-peak periods, while allocations optimized for average load consistently underperform during daily peak windows, violating SLAs and degrading user experience.

Sudden, unpredictable surges in traffic triggered by viral social media events, major product launches, or breaking news cycles can cause request rates to increase by orders of magnitude within seconds. The typical provisioning latency of 2-5 minutes for GPU instances is wholly inadequate when service quality collapses within the first 30 seconds of a spike.

Unlike conventional web requests with uniform processing times, LLM requests vary enormously in computational complexity. A simple factual query may require only a handful of output tokens and complete in milliseconds, while a complex code generation task may demand thousands of tokens. This extreme heterogeneity makes resource planning and batch scheduling significantly more challenging.

Certain LLM applications experience predictable seasonal demand patterns -such as increased usage during tax preparation season for financial AI tools -while others are subject to irregular, event-driven spikes that are fundamentally difficult to anticipate from historical data alone.

Despite significant recent advances in LLM inference optimization, existing serving frameworks and cloud management tools fall critically short in addressing the full complexity of variable traffic management for production LLM workloads.

• Static Deployment Approaches allocate a fixed number of GPU instances regardless of traffic conditions. While operationally simple, they are either wasteful during low traffic or become bottlenecks during surges.

• Reactive Auto-Scaling Systems such as Kubernetes HPA respond only after performance degradation has already occurred. End-to-end scaling latency of 2-8 minutes is categorically insufficient for flash crowd scenarios.

• Existing LLM Serving Frameworks such as vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, and DeepSpeed-MII optimize for steady-state performance but do not natively address dynamic traffic adaptation or proactive resource scaling.

• Cloud Cost Optimization Tools operate at a level of abstraction far removed from LLM-specific serving logic and cannot make intelligent real-time decisions about model variant selection or request priority routing.
This paper makes the following key and original contributions to the fields of cloud computing, machine learning systems, and large language model infrastructure:

1. AdaptServe Framework: A cloud-native LLM serving system integrating traffic-aware scheduling, adaptive dynamic batching, tiered model inference, and predictive proactive scaling into a unified production-ready framework.

2. Tiered Inference Architecture: A novel model-tiering strategy that dynamically routes requests between full-scale and lightweight distilled model variants based on real-time traffic load and request complexity.
